extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media studies; journalism educators and journalists interested in sociology of news organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria for how media routines and organizational structures shape news production and content, including source selection, access control, gatekeeping, and economic/ownership influences. Useful for evaluating why certain events are covered or framed the way they are in news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert source selection (succinct, predictable, centrist experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts are valued for their succinct and predictable responses, which reinforce conventional wisdom; centrist experts 'alleviate the need to balance' and are frequently and repeatedly quoted (Cooper & Soley, 1990; Ornstein).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers prefer sources who give predictable, brief commentary; repeat use of the same experts can become a routine practice (even banned temporarily by some editors) and creates audience appeal and an appearance of impartiality. Anti-pattern: Over-reliance on a narrow pool of predictable experts that narrows perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: University experts as devices to 'reinforce understanding' and create 'illusion of objective reporting'
rubrics_metrics.description: University experts are attractive to television news producers because they 'reinforce their own understanding of a story' and create 'the illusion of objective reporting' (Steele, 1990).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers call academics to round out stories since their commentary is presumed impartial; consequence is few academics provoke or challenge, yet their appearance suggests important analysis. Guidance for producers/editors: be aware that academic status is used rhetorically and does not guarantee independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source information management / manipulation of routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources regulate and shape the flow of information to make routines work in their favor (e.g., distancing the press, restricting questions, reducing unscripted encounters), a strategy developed into a PR model of information management under recent administrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include denying access, providing staged visuals, barring reporters (e.g., Grenada), or offering controlled briefings. For evaluators: examine how source-controlled access affected what reporters could gather and how that shaped coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distancing and access restriction (press-control techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple distancing of the press: using noisy helicopters to drown out questions, restricting questions at photo ops, drastically reducing press conferences, and barring reporters during operations (Grenada example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These techniques increase dependence on official messages and reduce opportunities for spontaneous questioning. Assess news output with attention to whether restricted access created information vacuums filled by source-provided narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripted spontaneity / minimizing press editing
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of 'scripted spontaneity' (originating with Nixon): before any public event, planners knew 'what the headline out of that event was going to be, what the picture was going to be, and what the lead paragraph would be...' (Smith, 1988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations/staff who allow staged events and pre-decided lines limit independent editorial shaping. Producers should watch for prepackaged narratives and assess whether material was designed to preempt network editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual press releases / crafted events
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Visual press release'—events crafted to make a visual message (e.g., Reagan visiting a job training center) designed to provide networks with irresistible events and craft the administration's story (Michael Deaver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are produced to be TV-friendly and to function as de facto programming for news shows. When evaluating footage, consider whether the event was staged to achieve a particular visual narrative rather than to inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to source bureaucracy / 'coupling of two information processing machines'
rubrics_metrics.description: News can be considered a product of one bureaucracy gathered from other bureaucracies; journalists adopt perspectives of the bureaucracies they cover, which highlights some occurrences while rendering others invisible (Sigal; Fishman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat structures and bureaucratic information flows condition reporters to see institutions from insiders' vantage points. To counteract this, editors can rotate beats or request reporters avoid routine ground rules promoted by sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat routines and reporters' 'rounds'
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters make systematic 'rounds' of locations (courts, sheriff, police) in an orderly, scheduled sequence to avoid wasting time; the beat routine is constructed around bureaucratic structure and yields the most efficient concentrations of information (Fishman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This efficiency produces predictable coverage but can miss atypical but newsworthy events ('nonevents' that interrupt bureaucratic flow). Evaluation should check whether beat routines caused omission of nonroutine stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional centers: 'media contact' and 'meeting' as concentrated information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists depend on two kinds of institutional centers: the 'media contact' (press representative) and the 'meeting', which concentrates lotsof information into a short period; these centers structure what becomes news (Fishman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories are often shaped by availability at meetings and official contacts rather than by independent investigation. Scrutinize whether coverage overweights what is easy to obtain from institutional centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pool reporting and wartime access constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Pool systems select representatives from major news organizations to accompany the military, obliging secrecy and subjecting reporters to military handlers and review by public information specialists (Persian Gulf War examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pool arrangements, military reviews, and handlers limit independent reporting and may bias accounts toward military frames. Analysts should account for how pool membership and military mediation shaped the reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-optation and rhetorical identification with sources (use of 'we', 'our')
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong dependence on sources can produce co-optation, signified by reporters' use of we/our (e.g., 'We invaded', 'our troops'), rhetorically binding anchors to military and national interests (Kellner, 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for language that aligns journalists with source frames; such phrasing can signal absorption of source definitions of success and marginalize alternative criteria (diplomatic, moral, environmental).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual/symbiotic routines and shared benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines developed that served mutual interests of media and military: the military got favorable demonstrations of weapons, the media got dramatic footage cheaply, and defense manufacturers got advertising—showing routines are practical for mutual benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating content, identify where mutual interests (access, footage, publicity) might have produced aligned incentives and thus constrained critical scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization as gatekeeper / multi-level editorial decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than single gatekeepers, the organization as a whole functions as a gatekeeper—a central nervous system with interdependent parts; exceptional cases (e.g., NBC's handling of the Loan execution film) show decisions engaged many organizational levels (Bailey & Lichty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess news selection by tracing organizational flows: which editors/producers/bureaus were involved, whose tastes and policies shaped the final decision, and when higher-level intervention overrode routine choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational roles (Who does what)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization charts show boxes representing roles and duties; as individuals are hired/promoted they take on duties/authorities associated with roles (e.g., owner/publisher, executive editor, editors, reporters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate coverage by identifying role responsibilities and how role assignments shape what work gets done and by whom. Consider specialization and whether role design affects editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational structure (How is the organization arranged?)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of boxes and connecting arrows indicates complexity—centralized vs. spread power, vertical connections, how departments are combined, and whether news departments are kept distinct to preserve autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine lines of authority and real vs. formal power (star columnists may be formally subordinate but practically independent). Structural analysis helps explain policy transmission and constraints on reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy content and implementation (What priorities and goals are set?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization charts don't show what policies are transmitted—what priorities are set and what goals are established; policy may come from the top and be implemented through various channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate stated policies and how they are implemented in practice; assess whether top-down priorities (audience appeal, profitability) dictated editorial choices on specific stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy enforcement (How are policies enforced?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts suggest questions about enforcement: how do executives ensure policies are carried out and what control do they have over workers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mechanisms of enforcement (budget control, hiring/firing, promotion) that mediate the balance between professional norms and organizational goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership, interlocks, and organizational boundaries affecting content
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations may be owned by nonmedia companies or have interlocks (shared boards/stock ownership) that complicate boundaries (e.g., GE owning NBC and being a defense contractor), affecting content decisions and constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ownership structures and interlocks to identify potential conflicts of interest and indirect pressures on editorial decisions. Question where organizational boundaries stop in networks of interlocking interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of economic goals / profit motive shaping organizational priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: For most organizations the primary goal is economic—to make a profit—which can override other goals such as public service or quality; publicly traded firms intensify the economic objective and managers face stockholder pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editorial decisions in light of profitability pressures: risk aversion by large firms, reluctance to publish material that might harm corporate interests, and centralized coordination across diversified holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economics as constraints on newswork (audience demand and advertising pressures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic considerations function as constraints on newswork—newsworkers find it hard to relate audience demand and advertising revenue to the nature and quality of news coverage (Sigal, 1973).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how budgetary decentralization or centralization affects story selection (e.g., which stories increase circulation/ratings) and whether economic constraints filter down to daily routines and beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role tensions between editors and reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are more audience-related whereas reporters are more source-related; different routines and requirements can bring them into conflict and must be reconciled, with organization goals ultimately prevailing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating newsroom output, identify these role-based tensions and whether editorial intervention (e.g., rotating beats, editorial directives) was used to mediate co-optation by sources.
